claims.statement: Randomized evidence on treating methamphetamine psychosis is limited: a 2009 Cochrane review found one eligible trial (58 participants), in which olanzapine and haloperidol were both effective and olanzapine caused fewer extrapyramidal side effects, and a later trial found haloperidol and quetiapine both effective; otherwise treatment rests on case reports and on evidence from other psychoses.
claims.magnitude: One trial (N=58) in the 2009 Cochrane review; one later trial; no placebo-controlled trial described.

claims.statement: Most methamphetamine-associated psychotic episodes described in the literature resolve within days to a month of stopping use, but a minority persist, and a substantial share of people hospitalized with methamphetamine psychosis later receive a schizophrenia diagnosis: figures cited second-hand in narrative reviews include 16–17% still psychotic after 1–3 months in two small studies, 10–28% beyond 6 months in hospital series, and 5% to about 39% later diagnosed with schizophrenia (about 39% within 5–6 years in a Thai cohort of more than 1,000). Recurrence with renewed use is common in clinical series.
claims.magnitude: Still psychotic after 1 and 3 months: 16% and 17% (two small studies from overlapping author groups); beyond 6 months 10–28%; later schizophrenia diagnosis 5.0% (China) to 38.8% at 5 years (Thailand; given as nearly 40% within 6 years in another review); 19.1–30% in register studies of amphetamine-induced psychosis.
